title: 47 Things to Check Before Moving Off Stripe Connect
summary: Considering a Stripe Connect alternative? Explore our 47-point migration checklist covering APIs, underwriting, payments, and launch.
body_markdown:
Migrating away from Stripe Connect is easy. You pick a new payments partner, flip a switch, move the data, and celebrate with tacos.


**Just kidding. Please do not do that.**


Moving payments infrastructure is less like switching your internet provider and more like replacing the plumbing in a hotel while every room is occupied. Money still has to move. Customers still expect their cards to work. Finance still expects the numbers to reconcile. Support would strongly prefer not to spend launch week explaining why something suddenly stopped working.


And engineering? Engineering would appreciate being included in this conversation


*before* someone announces a migration date.


So before anyone puts a giant red X through


**Stripe Connect** , here are 47 questions worth answering.


## First: Know What You’re Actually Migrating


Before debating APIs, tokenization or launch dates, document exactly what Stripe Connect is doing inside your platform today.


1. **Which Stripe Connect account model are you using?**


Standard, Express and Custom integrations can create very different migration considerations.


If your internal migration document just says “Stripe,” you’re already starting with a problem.


1. **Which payment flows depend on Stripe?**


Map every place money enters, leaves or moves through the platform.


Think beyond checkout.


Subscriptions. One-time payments. Refunds. Payouts. Fees. Adjustments. Disputes. Whatever your particular platform has built around payments.


You don’t want to discover an “Oh, Stripe handles that too?” three days before launch.


1. **What Stripe APIs does your application currently call?**


Inventory them.


Don’t rely on institutional memory, especially if the institution is one engineer named Kevin who built the integration four years ago.


1. **What webhooks are you consuming?**


Document every event your application listens for and what happens after it receives it.


A webhook isn’t particularly exciting until one disappears.


Then it becomes everyone’s favorite meeting.


1. **What internal systems depend on Stripe data?**


Your payments integration may feed more than your product.


Look for dependencies involving:


- CRM


- Accounting


- Customer support


- Reporting


- Fraud monitoring


- Business intelligence


- Billing


- Reconciliation


- Tax workflows


The migration boundary may be considerably larger than the payments team expects.


## The “What Happens to All Those Cards?” Section


And here we meet one of the more interesting parts of any payment migration:


Stored payment methods.


1. **How many customers have stored payment methods**


Know the scale before deciding how you’re going to move them.


1. **Where are those payment credentials actually stored?**


What looks like a saved card inside your application may actually be represented by a token or provider-specific identifier.


That distinction matters.


A lot.


1. **Can your existing payment credentials be migrated?**


Do not assume the answer is yes.


Determine exactly what can be transferred, under what conditions and through what process.


1. **Which identifiers are Stripe-specific?**


Create an inventory of the customer, account, payment-method and transaction identifiers your application relies on. Determine which references will need to change or be mapped in the new environment.


1. **Will customers have to re-enter payment information?**


This is one of the questions that can turn a technically successful migration into a spectacular customer-experience failure.


Find out early.


1. **How will recurring payments transition?**


Subscriptions do not care that your team is “between processors.”


They will attempt to bill right on schedule.


1. **What happens to payments scheduled during the migration window?**


Friday night at 11:59 PM is not a migration strategy.


Map the transition.


1. **How will expired or updated cards be handled?**


Consider what currently happens when stored credentials change and whether equivalent functionality exists in the new environment.


## Follow the Money


Eventually someone from finance is going to ask:


**“Okay, but where’s the money?”**


It is much better if the migration team has wondered the same thing.


1. **How are funds settled today?**


Document the existing flow from transaction to bank account.


1. **What will settlement look like after migration?**


“Basically the same” is not documentation.


1. **Will settlement timing change?**


If money arrives on a different schedule, treasury and finance need to know before launch, not during their first reconciliation.


1. **Which bank accounts receive funds?**


Verify accounts, ownership and routing.


1. **How are platform fees calculated?**


If monetizing payments is part of your business model, document your current economics before changing the infrastructure underneath them.


1. **Where are fees deducted?**


Gross settlement and net settlement can create very different reconciliation conversations.


1. **How will refunds affect settlement?**


Trace the entire accounting flow.


1. **What happens with negative balances?**


Happy-path diagrams are lovely.


Payments have an unfortunate habit of leaving the happy path.


1. **How are reserves handled?**


Understand whether reserve requirements or mechanics change with the new model.


## Underwriting: Everybody’s Favorite Party Topic


Nobody has ever shouted:


**“Let’s talk merchant underwriting!”**


at a cocktail party.


Nevertheless, if your SaaS platform supports merchants or connected businesses, this section matters enormously.


1. **Which customers require underwriting or verification?**


Define who is actually being onboarded into the new payments ecosystem.


1. **What merchant information do you already have?**


Inventory it before asking thousands of customers for information you’ve already collected.


1. **What additional information will the new provider require?**


Onboarding and verification requirements can differ between providers and programs.


Find the gaps.


1. **Can existing information be reused?**


Determine what can legitimately move into the new onboarding process and what must be collected or verified again.


1. **Who owns the merchant onboarding experience?**


You?


Your payments provider?


Both?


“Sort of both” is usually where things become interesting.


1. **What happens when underwriting or verification fails?**


Your migration plan needs an exception path.


Not every account will necessarily sail through.


1. **How will exceptions be handled?**


Define who investigates them, who communicates with the customer and what happens to payment functionality in the meantime.


## Reconciliation: Where Optimism Goes to Die


Your new system processed $1,000.


Your bank account received $943.16.


**Congratulations. You now have a reconciliation project.**


1. **How do you reconcile Stripe transactions today?**


Document the current process before attempting to reproduce or improve it.


1. **What identifiers connect transactions to settlements?**


Your teams need a reliable trail from payment to payout to bank deposit.


1. **Will transaction IDs change?**


If downstream systems rely on Stripe identifiers, identify those dependencies before they break.


1. **How will fees appear in reports?**


Finance should know how processing costs and other deductions will be represented.


1. **How will refunds appear?**


Same question.


Different headache.


1. **How will disputes and chargebacks appear?**


Determine how these events will be tracked and reconciled in the new environment.


1. **Can accounting recreate its existing reports?**


Don’t wait until month-end to discover the answer is “not exactly.”


## Now Let Engineering Ruin Everyone’s Timeline


Actually, let engineering


**save** the timeline.


They’re the people most likely to spot the hidden dependency everyone else missed.


1. **What development environments are required?**


Make sure engineering has access to the appropriate test environment, documentation and credentials well before launch.


1. **Have API differences been mapped?**


Create a direct comparison between the existing implementation and the replacement architecture.


1. **Have webhook behaviors been mapped?**


Events, payloads, timing, retries and downstream actions all deserve attention.


“Both systems have webhooks” doesn’t mean both systems behave identically.


1. **Have failure scenarios been tested?**


Don’t just test:


Customer pays. Payment succeeds. Everybody applauds.


Test the ugly stuff.


Declines. Timeouts. Duplicate requests. Interrupted connections. Failed payouts. Refunds. Exceptions.


Launch day has an uncanny ability to locate whichever scenario you didn’t test.


1. **Have you tested real-world transaction volumes?**


A development environment behaving beautifully with 12 transactions is encouraging.


It is not load testing.


1. **Is there a rollback or contingency plan?**


If something goes sideways, can you stop?


Can you revert?


Can you temporarily route transactions differently?


Know the answer before you need it.


## Please Tell Your Customers


One group has been suspiciously absent from this migration so far:


**Your customers.**


1. **Which customers will notice the change?**


Some migrations can happen primarily behind the scenes.


Others may require onboarding steps, new payment information, changed reporting, updated terms or operational changes.


Segment accordingly.


1. **What does the customer actually need to do?**


Be brutally specific.


If the answer is nothing, wonderful.


If the answer is something, make that something painfully easy to understand.


1. **Who gets notified and when?**


Customers, customer support, finance, sales, account management and implementation teams may all need different information.


One companywide email titled


**IMPORTANT PAYMENT UPDATE** is probably not the communications plan you’re looking for.


## Launch Week: Everybody Remain Calm


You tested.


You documented.


You reconciled.


You held meetings about meetings.


Now you’re ready.


Almost.


1. **What will you monitor after cutover?**


Decide before launch which indicators will tell you whether the migration is actually healthy.


Watch the areas that matter to your implementation, such as successful transactions, declines, funding, payouts, onboarding exceptions, refunds and reconciliation.


And decide


**who is watching what** .


A dashboard without an owner is just a very expensive screen saver.


1. **Who has the authority to yell “STOP”?**


This may be the most important question on the entire list.


If transactions begin failing, reconciliation doesn’t match or money isn’t landing where expected, everyone should know:


- Who makes the decision


- What triggers that decision


- Who gets contacted


- What happens next


Because the middle of a payments migration is a terrible time to discover that six people thought someone else was in charge.


## The Question Isn’t “Can We Leave Stripe Connect?”


Of course you can evaluate alternatives.


The better question is:


**Can you move without breaking the experience you’ve spent years building?**


That’s where payment migrations become interesting.


The processor is only one piece.


You also have stored payment methods, provider-specific identifiers, APIs, webhooks, connected accounts, underwriting, settlement, reconciliation, reporting, finance operations and customers who would strongly prefer not to know that any of this is happening.


A successful migration isn’t the one with the prettiest architecture diagram.


It’s the one where the new infrastructure goes live and customers collectively say:


**“Wait. You changed something?”**


Exactly.


## Thinking About Moving Off Stripe Connect?


This is where Usio enters the conversation.


Usio works with vertical SaaS platforms and ISVs processing payments in the U.S. For companies focused primarily on domestic payments, that creates an important question:


**If you’re not building a global eCommerce marketplace, do you need a payments platform designed to support one?**


The better question may be whether your payments infrastructure fits the business you’re actually running: how you accept payments, how money moves, how merchants are onboarded, how transactions are reconciled and how your platform makes money from payments.


## Can You Use Stripe and Usio?


**Absolutely. It doesn’t have to be an either-or decision.**


A SaaS platform with both U.S. and international payment requirements may choose different providers for different parts of its payments strategy. Stripe can remain part of the architecture where it makes sense, while Usio can be evaluated for U.S. payment processing.


The question isn’t necessarily,


**“How do we get rid of Stripe?”**


It’s:


**“Where does Stripe make sense, where does Usio make sense, and what architecture gives our business the best economics and payment experience?”**


## Start With the Migration, Not the Sales Pitch


Instead of beginning with:


**“Here’s why we’re better.”**


Begin with the much more useful question:


**“What would it actually take to move?”**


That’s a conversation worth having.
